title: Seamless Tier × CRM-Connect Analysis
headline: Killed a planned UI investment and reframed the growth bet from 'more Free signups' to 'CRM-connect the Basic base'
summary: First analysis shipped at Seamless.AI. Segmented ~590K searches by license tier and CRM-connection status to find where monetizable value actually accrued, and where it didn't.
problem: Leadership believed Free-tier acquisition was the growth lever. My job: test that against ~590K real searches.
strategy:
Segment every search by license tier (Free / Basic / Premium), crossed with CRM-connection status. CRM-connection is the proxy for monetizable signal, since Free is locked out of CRM by design.

One chart, one question: where does the value live, and where is it being left on the table?
insights:
Free drove the most volume (~159K searches) but zero monetizable signal by definition.

Basic was the real battleground. Searches split ~50/50 connected vs not (~111K / ~102K). Half the paying Basic base never wired up the revenue-driving integration.

Premium was overwhelmingly connected (~65K / ~22K), proving the upgrade path monetizes. A parallel filter-usage cut killed the planned advanced-filter UI. Usage was flat across tiers; no Premium 'power user' pattern existed.
outcome: Killed the planned advanced-filter UI. Reframed growth from 'more Free signups' to 'CRM-connect the Basic base'. That became the baseline through the next planning cycle.

title: Seamless API — Consumption Forecast
headline: Built the credit-consumption forecast behind a $1M-ARR API launch; the model still drives the next-tier sales plan
summary: Stood up the analytics and forecasting behind a customer-facing API from zero to $1M ARR. Every scope call was anchored to one metric: async credit consumption. The year-two MoM run-rate forecast informs enterprise expansion planning.
problem: Stand up a net-new, customer-facing API and prove the revenue model with data before scaling coverage.
strategy:
Anchor every scope call to one metric: async credit consumption, because credits are how the API monetizes.

Stood up a MoM credit-consumption and ARR run-rate forecast in Power BI to size the enterprise wedge and pace the rollout.

Instrumented the usage funnel end-to-end so adoption, activation, and consumption were measurable from day one.
insights:
Internal developer interviews surfaced reconciliation gaps in how credits were counted. Competitive analysis informed the metric framing.

Deliberately de-scoped features that didn't consume credits, since they couldn't move the metric the MVP existed to prove.

The forecast model surfaced that mid-market credit velocity was outpacing the SMB curve, redirecting go-to-market toward mid-market sooner than the original plan.
outcome: $1M booked ARR in year one. The credit-consumption forecast became the basis of the year-two sales plan.
tradeOff:
Scoping the analytics around research and search (and explicitly excluding Connect-integration usage) was the right call to prove the revenue model fast. The side effect: Connect started reading as a non-core surface in the data.

The bill came due at MCP. Because the Connect paths hadn't been exercised through the API contract from day one, retrofitting them — and instrumenting them — got materially more involved. Right call at the time. More work down the line.

title: Data Engine 4.0
headline: 20% lower AWS spend, deduped data, safe incremental refresh
summary: Rebuilt the Seamless.AI Data Engine end-to-end: ingestion, identity resolution, the star-schema semantic layer, and refresh cadence. Better coverage, deduped data, and 20% lower AWS spend in the first three months.
problem: The Data Engine's contact data was duplicated and expensive to refresh. Coverage was slipping, unit cost was climbing, and incremental refresh wasn't safe because keys weren't stable.
strategy:
Treat it as a pipeline rebuild, not a patch.

Source → ingestion (S3 + staging) → transformation (dbt models on Snowflake) → a star-schema semantic layer → BI and API consumption. Each stage instrumented for delivery time, quality, dedupe rate, and unit cost.

Re-keyed every dimension around a stable surrogate key so incremental refresh could run safely instead of full rebuilds.

Replaced the old identity-resolution pass with a deterministic-first, then fuzzy, match strategy validated before promotion.
insights:
Stakeholder interviews on prior releases and Data Engineering leadership surfaced the re-architecture and cost-saving opportunities.

The new dedupe logic was validated via champion/challenger: old and new identity-resolution passes ran against a labeled sample, with false-merge and miss rates measured before promotion.

Moving from full refreshes to surrogate-key incremental refresh is where most of the 20% AWS savings came from — far less compute reprocessing unchanged rows.

Processing tens of millions of contact records per cycle, the pipeline was made idempotent: a failed or re-run batch lands the same rows, so retries never double-count or corrupt the warehouse.
outcome: Higher contact coverage, a stable unique-ID system for updates over time, safe incremental refresh, and 20% lower AWS spend in the first three months.

title: Seamless MCP
headline: Launched on GPT + Claude in one quarter
summary: Shipped API 2.0 alongside MCP on the GPT and Claude stores in a single quarter, exposing the full Seamless data surface to agents without a custom integration per platform.
problem: Expose Seamless data and search to modern AI platforms without building and maintaining a custom integration per platform.
strategy:
Use MCP as a single, standard surface instead of building custom agent integrations per platform.

Same data surface area, a fraction of the build and maintenance cost.
insights:
Conversations with senior AI engineers identified MCP as the most efficient path versus custom automation.

Defined the data contract and functional requirements; engineering implemented against them.
outcome: Simultaneous launch of API 2.0 and MCP on the GPT and Claude stores, exposing the full Seamless feature set.

title: Seamless Fast Data
headline: 15x faster execution, 30% less compute
summary: Cut data lag from twice-monthly to every two hours by reworking the change-data pipeline across event broker, real-time processing, and the warehouse.
problem: Shrink the lag between updated data hitting the lake and going live in-app.
strategy:
Focus on the highest-demand attributes first: job changes and individual contact name updates.

De-scoped real-time ingest of corporate structure and acquisitions. Demand signal was weak and pipeline cost didn't justify it.
insights: Mapped the change-data flow across event broker, real-time processing, cloud storage, and the data warehouse to identify the highest-leverage transformations.
outcome: Twice-monthly to every two hours, zero downtime. 15x faster execution, 30% less compute.

title: Inseego Connect — Sales BI Model
headline: $1M+ ARR uplift via GTM re-targeting. Model still in production
summary: Power BI semantic model on government contracts. Still in production; sales leadership reviews it weekly, and it drives ongoing IoT targeting decisions.
problem: Inseego IoT was underperforming in the Connect partner channel. Sales needed an always-on view of where IoT actually belonged, not a one-off slide.
strategy:
Build a recurring BI artifact, not a slide deck.

Python ETL into a star-schema semantic model (contracts → segments → products), with surrogate keys for incremental refresh. RLS by sales region so each rep only sees their book.

DAX measures for contract-value share and IoT attach rate, published to a workspace sales leadership reviews weekly.
insights:
The model surfaced that the highest-value Connect contracts were almost entirely phone provisioning, not IoT.

Smaller state-level contracts had far more IoT buying power. We'd been pushing IoT at the wrong segment.

Because the model refreshes incrementally, the same insight kept compounding as new contract data landed, driving state-level targeting decisions across California and New York.
outcome: $1M+ ARR uplift in the first re-targeting cycle. Still the system of record for IoT-vs-phone contract mix. Referenced in QBRs and cloned by adjacent teams.

title: Latin Hyper-Texts
headline: Designed the relational data architecture behind a research platform still in active scholarly use
summary: Relational database and metadata architecture for annotating digitized Latin manuscripts, built to be maintained by the non-technical researchers using it.
problem: Give students a platform to research, annotate, and collaborate on digitized Latin manuscripts, with a data model maintainable by non-technical users.
strategy:
Divide and conquer.

Design a full relational database with image hosting and a metadata model, then integrate an existing digital annotation tool — all maintainable by low-tech students.
insights:
Qualtrics surveys after every training session shaped the data model and UX.

Competitive analysis informed hosting and database tooling choices.
outcome: Student-managed manuscript database, integrated with Digital Mappa. Adopted by the Butler School of Music as primary-source research infrastructure.

title: Arc of Southern Maryland — Service Operations Analytics
headline: −1 FTE billing headcount, 46% faster service throughput, auto-SLA on every record
summary: Service Operations Analytics build for Arc of Southern Maryland, delivered as a CaseWorthy client engagement: cohort-tracked throughput, automated billing-rule validation, and an exec ops dashboard that absorbed one full FTE of manual reconciliation.
problem: Arc's service-delivery org ran on spreadsheets. Billing reconciliation ate a full FTE, course turnaround was opaque, and leadership had no recurring throughput view.
role: Operations Analyst & Implementation Owner · CaseWorthy engagement at Arc of Southern Maryland
strategy:
Treat it as an ops-analytics build, not a system rollout.

Map the service-delivery funnel (intake → enrollment → course completion → billing) end-to-end and instrument each stage.

Stand up a recurring dashboard leadership reviews on the same cadence as payroll, and auto-validate every record against billing rules at point of entry. Exceptions surface before they hit the queue, not after.
insights:
Cohort throughput by program revealed which courses bottlenecked turnaround. The 46% gain came from targeting those, not a blanket process change.

The billing-rule validation layer turned reconciliation from a downstream cleanup task into an upstream gate, which is what eliminated the FTE.

Low-friction UX kept training cost near zero, so ops gains weren't eaten back by adoption drag.
outcome: −1 FTE of billing reconciliation. 46% faster course turnaround. Every record auto-validated against billing rules before it hits the queue.
